hook: A district says 70% of its high schoolers ride the bus but only 55% of its middle schoolers do. A reporter checks with two random samples and gets a gap of 0.02 instead of 0.15. Is the district wrong, or is that just what samples do? To answer, you need to know how a difference of two sample proportions behaves from sample to sample.

prereq.q: A population has $p = 0.4$. What is the standard deviation of $\hat{p}$ for random samples of 100?
For $n = 50$ and $p = 0.1$, is the large counts condition met?
prereq.why: Both $np$ and $n(1 - p)$ must be at least 10; $np = 5$ fails.

prereq.q: A normal distribution has mean 0.15 and standard deviation 0.05. What is the z-score of 0.05?

figure.caption: 1,000 simulated values of $\hat{p}_A - \hat{p}_B$ with the normal curve the formulas predict: mean 0.14, standard deviation 0.060.

chain.cause: Take a random sample from each of two populations, independently
chain.effect: each sample proportion has its own chance error, and so does their difference $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$

chain.cause: Each sample proportion is centered at its true proportion
chain.effect: the difference is centered at $p_1 - p_2$, so it is an unbiased estimator of the true difference

chain.cause: The two chance errors come from separate samples and do not cancel
chain.effect: the variances add: $\sigma^2 = \frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}$, and the standard deviation is its square root

chain.cause: Both samples have at least 10 expected successes and 10 expected failures
chain.effect: the sampling distribution is approximately normal, so z-scores and normal areas give probabilities

ideas: Standard deviation: $\sigma_{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2} = \sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}}$. Add variances, never standard deviations.
Shape: approximately normal when $n_1 p_1$, $n_1(1-p_1)$, $n_2 p_2$ and $n_2(1-p_2)$ are each at least 10.
Conditions: two independent random samples (or two randomly assigned groups), and each sample less than 10% of its population when sampling without replacement.

misconception.wrong: Subtracting the sample proportions means you subtract their standard deviations too, so the difference varies less than either one.
misconception.right: Each sample brings its own chance error, and the errors add up rather than cancel. The variances add, so a difference varies more than either sample proportion alone.

summary: For two independent random samples, $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$ is centered at $p_1 - p_2$ and has standard deviation $\sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}}$: the variances add. When all four large counts are at least 10, its distribution is approximately normal, so you can find probabilities with z-scores.
